newsitem.title: FINLAND: FINNISH 1996 JOBLESS RATE FELL TO 16.3 PCT -REPORT.
newsitem.headline: FINNISH 1996 JOBLESS RATE FELL TO 16.3 PCT -REPORT.

text.p: The Finnish unemployment rate fell to on average 16.3 percent in 1996 from 17.2 percent in 1995, a government report said on Tuesday.
"Unemployment has fallen throughout 1996, but slower than expected," said the report complied by a group of top-level government officials.

Annual economic growth projected at around four percent and already implemented employment measures and training schemes would make it possible to bring the jobless rate "close to 12 percent" by 1999, the report said.
That would be well above the government's target.
"And so reaching the target to halve unemployment will require additional measures," the report said.
Upon taking office in April 1995, the five-party government set as its top priority to halve the unemployment rate to 8-9 percent by the end of its term in 1999.
Reviewing the report on Tuesday, the government's economic policy minister committee reaffirmed that it thinks the jobless rate can be halved by 1999.
The report said employment may initially improve quicker than expected due to the fact that the emphasis of economic growth is now resting squarely on the domestic market.
"In 1996, the focus of the demand for labour shifted clearly to the domestic market along with increasing consumer demand," the report said.
The number of people at work in the service sector increased by 31,000 last year compared with a rise of 19,000 in 1995.
In trade and commerce, 14,000 new jobs -- an increase of 4.3 percent -- were created. But the banking and financing sector shed 3,000 jobs in 1996.
In industry, the number of people at work rose by 4,000 compared to a rise of 30,000 in 1995. New jobs were created only in the metal, engineering and electrotechnical industries.
The number of people at work in agriculture decreased by 8,000 in 1996 and the forestry sector shed 2,000 jobs.

In construction, the sharp rise late in 1996 in building permits and actual project start-ups did not have any significant impact on employment -- the number of people at work in construction increased by just 1,000, the report said.

But this year the revival in construction investments would boost employment by about 10,000 people, it said, adding this was expected to boost jobs creation in other sectors by almost the same amount.
Construction costs could rise too much, the report warned.

"A too rapid pace of growth in construction may lead to an uncontrolled rise in construction costs," it said. "Because of that there is no reason to strengthen the rise in investment by economic policy means," it added.
The boom in construction may even lead to labour shortages despite the big number of unemployed construction workers, the report said.
